newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks open hinges on CPI data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks open hinges on CPI data.

text.p: The January consumer price index, due out at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, will determine whether the Dow industrials extend their final-hour rally at the open or if investors will take profits.
Market players will also be looking at December international trade data for any indication whether the strong dollar has taken a bite out of exports.
"If the price data are any weaker than forecast, the market can continue its rally," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.

"If the data come in above and beyond expectations, bonds will weaken and that will send stocks lower. The international trade numbers will give us some insight into how the economy is doing and whether the strong dollar is creating problems for exports," Cardillo said.

Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities, said the opening was absolutely no indication of where the market would close, as programs have recently tended to kick in late and send the Dow higher.
A strong earnings report from Hewlett-Packard Co is expected to give the high tech sector a boost.

Among U.S. shares traded in London, Hewlett-Packard was up two at 51-1/2 following the after-hours release of its first quarter results. The company reported earnings per share of $0.87 compared with a First Call consensus estimate of $0.75 per share.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was up 13.4 at 4345.7.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average gained 128.37 points, or 0.69 percent, to close at 18,599.12.
The dollar was firm in Tokyo and held above 1.69 marks in choppy European trading.
U.S. Treasuries were mixed, with the long bond up 2/32 to yield 6.54 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that Internet stocks are making a comeback, led by the search engine companies which help people find information on the Internet and try to make money selling advertising.

The New York Times Market Place writes that H.F. Ahmanson and Co hopes to benefit from its unsolocited bid for Great Western Financial Corp by cutting thousands of jobs, closing 201 branches and shedding about $400 million a year in expenses.
